description: An amateur astronomer, AAVSO solar observer, astrophotographer, certified asteroid hunter and science communicator. I am passionate about citizen science, satellite data, astronomy outreach and applying space-based technologies to real-world challenges. Our team brings together an interest in Earth observation, agriculture, data analysis and technology to explore innovative solutions for sustainable farming.
summary: Desert Crop Navigator helps farmers in Jodhpur, Barmer and Sikar, three dry districts of Rajasthan, India, decide what to grow next. A farmer answers four short questions on a phone: where the field is, the usual monsoon and winter crops, water access, and soil. The app then rates crops for the coming season and compares three rotation plans: what the farmer grows now, a plan that saves water, and a plan that builds soil. Each plan explains why it was suggested, the evidence, benefits, what we do not know, and what to check with the local Krishi Vigyan Kendra (farm science center). NASA POWER rainfall, heat and soil wetness, and NASA HLS satellite greenness, drive the ratings. For example, 2026 has had only 60 to 70% of the usual rain so far, so low-water crops rate higher. The app works in Hindi and English, offline after the first visit, and makes a PDF farm report to share. It supports farmers' judgement; it does not replace it.
details:
What does it do?

Desert crop Navigator combines three different functions:

  1. Agricultural decision support – crop suitability and rotation options.
  2. Environmental monitoring – rainfall, temperature, soil moisture and vegetation indicators.
  3. Farm information and economics – farmer profile, soil-test details and user-entered financial calculations.
  • Four-step start for farmers with little technical knowledge : big picture buttons, few words, language option (Hindi or English).
    1. Location: "Use my location" (rounded to about 10 km) or tap a district.
    2. Usual crops: Crops that suit the area this year show as tiles ; "Other" opens a list with the rest, poor fits marked with the reason, and "Nothing (field left empty)" for winter.
    3. Water: Rain only, some irrigation, or enough irrigation.
    4. Soil: Sandy, loamy or heavy, and whether a white salt crust is seen or not.
  • Best crops for next season: Top 3 crops , with reasons, warnings and the usual district yield (Government of India data).
  • Three rotation plans compared, as the challenge asks: what you grow now, then under "Recommended crops": crops which save water and crops which build soil (with a legume). Each shows why, evidence, benefits, what we don't know, and what to check with the KVK.
  • What NASA sees near you: Rain this year versus a usual year, rain by month, days of 40 °C or more, usual soil moisture by month, field greenness by month, and a map with the district outline and the 10 km farmland squares where the data is read.
  • Crop decision rules: A visual explanation of the project's agricultural suitability rules and environmental indicators, along with the complete crop reference table.
  • All crop options: Only crops that are a Good fit for the field, plus a search to check any crop.
  • Optional details: Farming system, investment, credit, market, labour and risk; Soil Health Card numbers (organic carbon, pH, EC); and a money calculator using the farmer's own costs, yield and price.
  • My farm report: Field, farm details, soil test, money, best crops, what NASA sees, the three plans (best marked), things to watch, good practices and checks before changing crops; print or share as a PDF.
  • A menu on every page, works on low-cost Android phones, installs like an app, and designed to support offline access to application content and previously available information. Updated environmental data require an internet connection.

How it works

Data and satellite processing:

  • Agricultural sampling: One representative 10 km × 10 km farmland sampling area is selected for each district (Jodhpur, Barmer and Sikar), using ESA WorldCover 2021 to identify areas mostly covered by agricultural land.
  • NASA POWER: Provides rainfall, maximum temperature and root-zone soil wetness data from 2021 onwards. The application requests the latest available data when opened with an internet connection.
  • NASA HLS v2.0: Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 imagery is used to calculate NDVI (vegetation greenness) for the period from 2024 to November 2026. Cloud, shadow and snow-affected pixels are excluded during image processing.

These datasets provide environmental insights for the selected sampling areas, not direct measurements of individual farmers' fields or the entire districts.

  • Crop suitability ratings: The application uses a transparent, rule-based scoring system that considers crop water requirements in relation to the farmer's available water, soil type, salinity tolerance, previous crops and relevant environmental conditions.
  • The system also applies three environmental rules relating to dry-year conditions, the arid-zone agricultural context and rainfall variability.

Crops are classified as:

  • 3 points or more: Good Fit
  • 1–2 points: Possible
  • 0 points or less: Poor Fit

Each rating is accompanied by an explanation so that farmers can understand the reasoning behind the recommendation.

The rules are designed to make every rating understandable to farmers, transparent in its reasoning and open to validation by local agricultural experts. Farm-profile, soil-test and financial information is based on figures entered by the farmer; the application does not maintain its own market-price database.

Benefits

  • Farmers can explore crop options and understand how district-level environmental conditions may affect agricultural choices for the coming season.
  • Helps farmers explore crop options suited to the available water and soil conditions.
  • Highlights alternatives that may support water conservation and soil improvement.
  • Explains the reasoning, evidence and limitations behind crop recommendations.
  • Encourages farmers to consult local agricultural experts before changing their cropping practices.
  • Honest about limits: Every plan says what to check locally before changing crops.
  • NDVI interpretation: These are preliminary satellite-derived comparisons of post-monsoon vegetation greenness against the 2024–25 reference period.
  • They should be interpreted as indicators of vegetation change, not direct measurements of crop yield or plant health.

What we hope to achieve next

  • Check every crop rule with KVK and CAZRI experts,
  • Cross-check rainfall with IMD,
  • Add more districts,
  • And add NASA SMAP soil moisture and GPM rainfall.

Known limitations (also stated in the app)

  • The crop rules are starter rules, not yet checked by agriculture experts.
  • NASA POWER rain is a model estimate. NASA's usual rain for Jodhpur (about 469 mm a year) is higher than the official normal (263 mm, ICAR-CRIDA), so the app compares each year with NASA's own usual year.
  • Each district's data comes from one 10 km farmland area, which represent the selected sampling areas and should not be interpreted as measurements of an individual farmer's field or the entire district.
  • Greenness is refreshed with the data scripts (NASA Earthdata login), not live on the phone.

Tools and languages

  • App: one HTML/CSS/JavaScript file, no framework; Leaflet map; offline service worker; hosted on Netlify.
  • Data processing: Python with earthaccess, rasterio, numpy and requests; charts with matplotlib.

What makes the project creative?

  • Desert Crop Navigator’s innovation lies in transforming complex Earth Observation (EO) data into simple, practical, and farmer-friendly insights that help farmers make more informed agricultural decisions.
  • Rather than just showing the raw satellite data, it brings in the climate indicators and the vegetation data and then provides a clear explanation of crop suitability.
  • Its three point comparison enables the farmer to look at their current practice along with two other ( water conservation and soil improvement).
  • The app also places a strong emphasis on explanation . A farmer can see why a particular crop has been recommended, what the evidence is for that recommendation and what are the risks involved.

What factors did we consider?

  • The project considers the environmental and practical conditions that affect agricultural decisions, including:
  • - District-level climatic differences.
  • - Rainfall variability and extended dry periods.
  • - Water availability and irrigation access.
  • - Soil type and potential salinity.
  • - Previous crops and crop rotation.
  • - Vegetation change as seen in the satellite imagery.
  • - Very easy to use for people with no technical experience at all.
  • - Accessible in Hindi and English.

Additional farmer and farm information

  • Farming system: Selection of the farming system, such as open-field cultivation.
  • Investment capacity: Indicates the farmer's available investment capacity.
  • Credit access: Records whether credit facilities are available.
  • Market access: Records the availability of nearby markets.
  • Labour availability: Captures the availability of farm labour.
  • Risk tolerance: Records the farmer's willingness to take agricultural risks.
  • Soil health parameters: Optional inputs for organic carbon (%), soil pH and electrical conductivity (EC), based on available Soil Health Card or soil-test reports.
  • Farm economics: Allows farmers to enter cultivated area, cultivation cost per acre, expected yield per acre, expected selling price and capital investment details.
  • Financial calculations: Performs basic arithmetic using figures entered by the farmer. It does not provide market prices, predict yields or guarantee financial returns.

DesertCrop Navigator is an attempt to bridge the gap between Earth Observation, climate information, agricultural knowledge and practical farmer decision-making.

The idea is making complex satellite information understandable and useful through a simple interface, while being transparent about the evidence, limitations and risks.

Our vision: NASA data in a farmer's pocket, in their own language.
